children.note: Plants need 17 elements; nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are the three needed in the largest amounts from soil. This map explains what each does, how it behaves in soil, how to read shortage or excess, and how organic farms supply and budget them with manures, rock minerals, legumes and microbes.

Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed in moderate amounts; eight micronutrients in tiny amounts, plus silicon as a useful extra. Shortages are often caused by soil pH rather than a true lack, so fixing pH and organic matter comes first.

Plants show nutrient shortages through colour, shape and where on the plant the damage starts. Learning to read these signs, then confirming with a soil or leaf test, lets you choose the right compost, mineral or microbe instead of guessing.

Organic fertilisers are manures, cakes, meals, green manures and natural minerals that feed crops through soil life. This map covers each source, how to calculate rates, storage, safety and what organic standards allow.

Biostimulants are substances and microbes that help crops use nutrients, tolerate stress or improve quality, without being fertilisers or pesticides. This map covers the main types, how they work, the evidence, how to use them and which are allowed in organic farming.

children.note: An element is essential when the plant cannot complete its life cycle without it and no other element can take its place.

children.topic: C, H, O: from air and water
children.note: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen make up most of plant dry matter. They come from carbon dioxide and water, not from fertilizer.

manas.q: Which three essential elements do plants get from air and water rather than soil?

children.note: Needed in large amounts and most often short in farm soils. They are the three numbers on a fertilizer label.
Needed in fairly large amounts but less often limiting. Covered in the "Secondary & Micronutrients" map.
Fe, Zn, Mn, B, Cu, Mo, Cl and Ni are needed in tiny amounts, yet a shortage of any one still limits yield.

manas.q: Name the eight micronutrients.

children.note: Growth is held back by whichever nutrient is shortest, like the lowest stave of a barrel. Adding more of a plentiful nutrient does not help.

manas.q: What does the "law of the minimum" say about plant growth?

children.topic: Mobile vs immobile in the plant
children.note: N, P and K move from old to new leaves, so their shortage shows first on older, lower leaves. This is the first clue when reading a sick plant.
The nutrient crops need most and the one most easily lost. It drives leafy growth and green colour.
Part of every protein, enzyme, DNA and chlorophyll molecule. Plenty of N means fast green growth; too little means small, pale plants.
Roots take N as nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+). Organic N in manure must first be broken down by microbes into these forms.

manas.q: In which two forms do roots take up nitrogen?

children.note: Microbes turn organic N into ammonium (mineralisation), then nitrate (nitrification). Nitrate is not held by soil particles, so it moves with water.
Heavy rain or over-irrigation washes nitrate below the root zone, especially on sandy soils. Cover crops can cut this loss.

links.label: 📄 Cover crops and N leaching review (Global Change Biol. 2019)

children.note: Ammonia gas escapes from manure or urine left on the surface, worst when warm, windy and on alkaline soil. Cover or incorporate manure quickly.
In waterlogged soil, bacteria turn nitrate into nitrogen gases that escape to the air. Good drainage limits this.

manas.q: What happens to nitrate in waterlogged soil?

children.note: Microbes eating straw or sawdust with a high carbon-to-nitrogen ratio lock up soil N for a while, so the crop turns pale. Compost such materials first.

manas.q: Why can fresh straw dug into soil make a crop turn yellow?

children.note: Older leaves turn evenly pale yellow first, plants are stunted with thin stems. In maize the yellowing runs as a V from the leaf tip along the midrib.

manas.q: What do nitrogen-deficient maize leaves look like?

children.note: Very dark, soft, lush leaves, delayed flowering and maturity, lodging, and more aphids and diseases. Leafy vegetables may hold high nitrate.
Low organic matter, sandy soils after heavy rain, waterlogging, cold soils that slow microbes, and high-carbon residues dug in.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Crops use only about half of the N applied worldwide; the rest is lost to water and air. Matching supply to crop demand is the key fix.

links.label: 📄 Nitrogen use efficiency review (Front. Plant Sci. 2023)

children.note: The energy nutrient. Soils often hold plenty of total P, but little of it is in a form roots can take up.
Part of ATP (the energy carrier), DNA and cell membranes. Vital for root growth, flowering, seed set and early vigour.
Roots take up phosphate ions (H2PO4- and HPO4 2-) dissolved in soil water. Concentrations in soil water are very low.
Phosphate binds to iron and aluminium in acid soils and to calcium in alkaline soils, becoming locked up. It is most available near pH 6–7.

manas.q: Why is phosphorus often unavailable in both very acid and alkaline soils?

children.note: P moves only a few millimetres to roots, so it hardly leaches. Losses come mainly from erosion of topsoil and runoff, which also pollute water.

links.label: 📄 Global soil P loss by erosion (Nature Commun. 2020)

children.note: Stunted plants with dark green or purple-red older leaves, weak roots, poor tillering and late maturity. Most visible in young crops on cold soils.

manas.q: Which leaf colour is a classic sign of phosphorus shortage?

children.note: Rarely shows on the plant directly, but very high P can induce zinc and iron shortage. Heavy manure use can build P beyond crop need.
Strongly acid or calcareous soils, low organic matter, cold or dry soil, eroded fields, and poor root growth from compaction or nematodes.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: The quality and stress nutrient. It is not built into plant tissues but works dissolved in plant sap.
Controls stomata and water balance, activates many enzymes, moves sugars into grain and fruit. Helps drought, frost and disease tolerance.
Roots take up the potassium ion K+. It is held on clay and humus exchange sites and released into soil water.
Some clays trap K between their layers (fixation) and release it slowly. On sandy, low-clay soils K can leach under high rainfall.

manas.q: Where is potassium held in soil?

children.note: Older leaves scorch and brown along the margins and tips while the centre stays green. Weak stalks, lodging, small fruit and poor storage.

manas.q: Where on the plant does potassium deficiency show first, and how?

children.note: Plants take up more K than they need ("luxury uptake"). Too much K competes with magnesium and calcium uptake and can cause Mg deficiency.

manas.q: Which nutrient shortage can heavy potassium use trigger?

children.note: Sandy or highly weathered soils, heavy cropping where straw and stover are removed, waterlogging, and dry topsoil.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Organic farms build fertility mainly from manures, compost, legumes and slow rock minerals. Nutrient content varies widely, so test local materials when you can.
Beans, cowpea, sunn hemp, Mucuna, dhaincha and clovers fix air N with Rhizobium. Cut and incorporate at early flowering for the most N.

manas.q: When should a green manure legume be cut and incorporated?

children.note: Supply N, P, K and organic matter. Fresh manure loses N as ammonia; well-stored or composted manure is safer and steadier.
Slow-release nutrients plus humus and microbes. Mainly a soil builder; supplies modest N per tonne compared with concentrated inputs.
Neem, castor, groundnut and karanj cakes are richer in N than manure and release it within weeks. Neem cake also slows nitrification.
Concentrated animal by-product N sources. Blood meal acts fairly fast; feather and horn meal release more slowly.
Ground natural phosphate rock. Dissolves slowly and works best in acid soils, or when composted or used with PSB.

manas.q: In which soils does rock phosphate work best?

children.note: Supplies P and calcium, released slowly. Some certifiers and buyers restrict animal by-products, so check rules.
Supplies K and calcium and raises pH like lime. Use thin amounts, never from painted or treated wood, and avoid on alkaline soils.

manas.q: Besides potassium, what does wood ash do to soil pH?

children.note: Allowed in organic farming only from natural mined sources with physical processing. Check your certifier before buying.
Supplies K and trace elements plus growth-active compounds. Low in N and P, so a supplement rather than the main source.
Synthetic urea, DAP, MOP processed with chemicals and other manufactured soluble fertilizers are not permitted under organic certification.

manas.q: Is urea allowed under organic certification?

children.note: Microbes make soil nutrients available; they complement manures but do not replace a real shortage.
Rhizobium (legumes), Azotobacter, Azospirillum and Azolla with blue-green algae add N from the air. See their own maps.
Phosphate-solubilising bacteria and fungi release organic acids and enzymes that free locked P. Best paired with rock phosphate or manure.

manas.q: How do phosphate-solubilising bacteria free locked phosphorus?

children.note: Potassium-mobilising bacteria help release K from soil minerals. Useful on low-K soils with organic matter; effects are modest.
AM fungi extend thin threads far beyond roots and bring back phosphate, especially in low-P soils.

manas.q: How do mycorrhizal fungi help phosphorus uptake?

links.label: 📄 AM fungi, PSB and silicon for P uptake (Front. Plant Sci. 2021)

children.note: Microbes need carbon, moisture and air. Regular organic matter, cover crops and little tillage keep them working.
Organic nutrients are released by microbes over weeks to months, so planning ahead matters more than quick fixes.
Apply manure or compost before planting and grow legumes in the season before. Crops need most N in the fast-growth phase.
Warm, moist soil releases N faster; cold, dry or waterlogged soil releases little. Early crops may still need a quick N source.

manas.q: Which soil conditions speed up release of N from organic matter?

children.note: Every harvest carries N, P and K off the farm. Grain removes much N and P; stover, straw and fruit carry away much K.
Add up nutrients brought in (manure, compost, feed, fixation) and subtract those sold. A long negative balance mines the soil.

manas.q: What is a farm nutrient balance?

children.note: In a Kenyan maize-vegetable trial, high-input organic plots showed positive partial N and K balances, higher than conventional plots at most sites.

links.label: 📄 Kenya organic vs conventional trial (Agric. Ecosyst. Environ. 2016)

children.note: Composting or mulching crop residues, recycling dung and urine, and avoiding burning keeps K and other nutrients on the farm.
A soil test checks whether P and K are rising or falling. Combine with leaf colour and yield records.
Common traps when managing N, P and K organically.
Excess manure builds up P and K, raises nitrate leaching risk and can unbalance Mg. Apply to crop need.
Yellowing can also come from waterlogging, S, Mg or Fe shortage, root disease or nematodes. Check leaf position and pattern.
Microbes help release and fix nutrients but cannot make P or K from nothing. They work best on soils with organic matter.

manas.q: Can biofertilizers replace manure and compost?

children.note: Digging in sawdust or straw just before planting locks up N. Compost first or add an N-rich source.

USGS — how N moves between air, soil, plants and water.

children.note: Sound Agriculture — why applied P gets locked up.
Soybean Science for Success — field look at K shortage symptoms.
UGA Extension — supplying N from legumes and manures in organic grain.

eOrganic webinar — planning nutrients for organic farms (long talk).

nodeData.note: Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed in moderate amounts; eight micronutrients in tiny amounts, plus silicon as a useful extra. Shortages are often caused by soil pH rather than a true lack, so fixing pH and organic matter comes first.

children.note: How to think about the "small" nutrients before reaching for a bag.
Micronutrients are needed in grams per hectare, yet one missing element can cut yield as much as a lack of N.
Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu and B become less available as pH rises above about 7. Mo is the opposite: it becomes more available as pH rises.

manas.q: Which micronutrient becomes MORE available as soil pH rises?

children.note: Below about pH 5.5, aluminium and manganese can reach toxic levels while Ca, Mg, P and Mo run short. Liming is the main fix.

manas.q: Which elements can become toxic in strongly acid soils?

children.note: Humus holds Ca, Mg and K, releases S and micronutrients, and forms natural chelates that keep Fe and Zn soluble.
For B, Cu and Mo the gap between too little and too much is small. Test before applying and never guess doses.
Needed in moderate amounts; often supplied with lime, dolomite and gypsum.
Builds cell walls and keeps membranes and growing tips healthy.
Glues cell walls together, keeps membranes stable, and is needed for root tips and fruit development. It barely moves inside the plant.
Young leaves and tips distorted or dying; blossom-end rot in tomato and pepper, tip-burn in cabbage and lettuce, bitter pit in apple.

manas.q: Which fruit disorder of tomato is linked to calcium supply?

children.note: Short on acid, leached and sandy soils. Often a supply problem from uneven watering, because Ca travels only with the water flow.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Rarely toxic, but very high Ca (calcareous soils) raises pH and locks up P, Fe, Zn and Mn.
Ground limestone (raises pH), gypsum (does not change pH), dolomite, bone meal, crushed eggshells, wood ash and compost.
The atom at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule.
Central atom of chlorophyll and an activator of many enzymes that handle energy and sugars.
Older leaves yellow between the veins while veins stay green, sometimes turning reddish. Leaves may drop early.

manas.q: Where does magnesium deficiency appear first, and what pattern does it make?

children.note: Short on acid, sandy, leached soils and where heavy K or ammonium applications compete with Mg uptake.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Rare; very high Mg relative to Ca can harm soil structure on some clays.
Dolomite (also raises pH), magnesium sulphate (Epsom salt, often allowed where need is shown), compost, manure.
Part of proteins and of the flavour and oil compounds in onion, garlic and mustard.
Builds the amino acids cysteine and methionine, needed for proteins, and helps nodules fix N in legumes.
Whole young leaves turn pale yellow, unlike N shortage which starts on old leaves. Oilseeds and legumes suffer most.

manas.q: How can you tell sulphur from nitrogen shortage by leaf position?

children.note: Short on low organic matter, sandy and leached soils, far from industrial air pollution. Most soil S is held in organic matter.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Excess sulphate is rarely a problem; elemental S used too heavily can make soil too acid.
Gypsum, elemental sulphur (acidifies; oxidised by soil bacteria), Epsom salt, sulphate of potash, compost and manure.
Iron, zinc, manganese, boron, copper, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel.
Needed to make chlorophyll; shortage is usually a lock-out, not a lack.
Needed to build chlorophyll and for enzymes in photosynthesis and respiration.
Youngest leaves turn yellow to white between sharply green veins; old leaves stay green.

manas.q: Why is iron chlorosis usually a lock-out rather than a lack of iron?

children.note: Common on calcareous, alkaline, over-limed or waterlogged soils, even though total soil iron is high.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: In flooded acid rice soils, too much soluble iron causes bronzing and brown spots on leaves.
Compost and manure (natural chelates), acidifying with sulphur on alkaline soils, and iron sulphate foliar sprays where permitted.
The most widespread micronutrient shortage in crops worldwide, common in India.
Activates enzymes, helps make the growth hormone auxin, and is needed for proper leaf expansion.
Small narrow leaves crowded in rosettes, short internodes, pale bands; "khaira" in rice and white bud in maize.

manas.q: What is "khaira" disease of rice?

children.note: Short on alkaline, calcareous, low organic matter, flooded or heavily P-fertilised soils.

manas.q: Which heavy input can induce zinc shortage?

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Toxicity is uncommon, mainly near mines or from heavy sludge use.
Zinc sulphate where permitted with a documented shortage, compost, manure and zinc-solubilising bacteria.
Works in the part of photosynthesis that splits water.
Needed to split water in photosynthesis and for several enzymes.
Young leaves show interveinal yellowing with small dead spots; grey speck in oats.
Short on high-pH, sandy or very high organic matter soils; more available when acid or waterlogged.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Toxic on strongly acid or waterlogged soils: brown spots and crinkled leaves. Liming fixes it.
Compost, acidifying alkaline soils, manganese sulphate foliar sprays where permitted.
Needed for cell walls, pollen and fruit set.
Builds cell walls, helps pollen tubes grow and moves sugars. Barely moves in the plant.
Growing points die, flowers drop, fruit cracks or deforms; hollow stem in cauliflower and broccoli.

manas.q: Why must boron be applied with great care?

children.note: Short on sandy, leached, low organic matter or limed soils, and in dry spells.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Toxic at levels only a little above need: leaf edges burn on older leaves. Never overdose.
Borax or boric acid in small, even amounts where permitted, compost and manure.
Needed for enzymes and for making lignin in stems.
Part of enzymes in photosynthesis and helps make lignin, so stems stay strong.
Young leaves wilt, twist or have white tips; cereal ears fail to fill; dieback of shoots.
Short on peat and very high organic matter soils and on sandy leached soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Builds up in soils after years of copper fungicide sprays, harming earthworms and roots.
Compost and manure; copper sulphate only with a documented shortage. Copper fungicides are allowed in organic but with limits.
Needed in the tiniest amount; vital for legumes and brassicas.
Part of the enzymes that reduce nitrate and that fix N in nodules.
Pale, N-deficiency-like leaves in legumes; "whiptail" (narrow, strap-like leaves) in cauliflower.

manas.q: Which cauliflower disorder is caused by molybdenum shortage?

children.note: Short on acid soils; liming often cures it. Unlike other micronutrients, high pH increases availability.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Excess in forage can harm grazing cattle by causing copper deficiency.
Liming acid soils; seed treatment with a small dose of sodium or ammonium molybdate where permitted.
Needed for water balance and photosynthesis. Shortage is very rare because rain and dust supply enough; excess from salty water or chloride salts is more common.
Part of urease, the enzyme that breaks down urea. Shortage is rare; "mouse-ear" leaves in pecan are a known case.

manas.q: Which enzyme needs nickel?

children.note: Not essential but useful, especially for rice, sugarcane and grasses.
Strengthens cell walls, making leaves stiffer and harder for insects and fungi to attack. Helps under drought, salt and metal stress.

links.label: 📄 Silicon and plant stress tolerance review (3 Biotech 2019)

children.note: Rice husk ash, rice straw returned to the field, and some rock dusts. Long-term straw removal depletes soil silicon.
Common inputs and what they supply. Always confirm with your certifier and use only with a soil or tissue test showing need.
Ground limestone supplies Ca and raises pH. Quicklime and slaked lime are generally not allowed as soil inputs.

manas.q: Which liming materials are allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Supplies both Ca and Mg and raises pH. Good where both are low; avoid where Mg is already high.
Supplies Ca and S without raising pH. Useful for groundnut pod filling and for sodic soils.

manas.q: What does gypsum supply, and does it raise pH?

children.note: Magnesium sulphate: quick Mg and S, as soil or foliar spray. Many standards allow it where a shortage is documented.
Slowly turned into sulphate by soil bacteria. Lowers pH on alkaline soils and supplies S.
Zinc, iron, manganese and copper sulphates and borax are allowed in many standards only with a documented deficiency.
Seaweed supplies trace elements and growth substances; compost supplies a balanced mix in small amounts.
Microbes that make secondary and micronutrients available.
Pseudomonas and Bacillus release siderophores, molecules that grab iron and make it available while denying it to pathogens.

manas.q: What is a siderophore?

children.note: Release acids that dissolve zinc oxide and carbonate in soil. Trials in wheat show better Zn uptake and grain Zn.

links.label: 📄 Zinc-solubilising rhizobacteria in wheat (Front. Plant Sci. 2022)

children.note: Thiobacillus species turn elemental sulphur into plant-available sulphate.
AM fungi help roots take up Zn and Cu as well as P.
Sprays correct shortages quickly but do not fix the soil cause.
For a confirmed shortage during the season, or when soil pH locks the nutrient out. Zn, Fe, Mn and B respond well.
Spray dilute solutions in the cool morning or evening, wet both leaf sides, and test on a few plants first.

manas.q: When is the best time of day to apply a foliar spray?

children.note: Some standards allow natural chelating agents such as lignosulphonate; check whether synthetic chelates are permitted.
Repeated foliar sprays treat symptoms. Fix pH, organic matter and drainage for lasting results.
Common traps with secondary and micronutrients.
Adding B, Cu or Zn without a test can easily cause toxicity that lasts for years.
Spraying iron on a high-pH soil every season treats the symptom; lowering pH or adding organic matter treats the cause.
Copper fungicides are allowed in organic farming, but the EU caps them at 28 kg Cu per ha over 7 years.

manas.q: How much copper does EU organic regulation allow?

links.label: 📄 EU rule limiting copper use, Reg. 2018/1981

children.note: Regional patterns worth knowing.
Many high-rainfall highland soils are acid, causing low P, Ca, Mg and Mo. Soil testing and liming are widely promoted.
Zinc shortage is widespread in Indian soils, followed by sulphur and boron. The Soil Health Card scheme tests micronutrients.

nodeData.note: Plants show nutrient shortages through colour, shape and where on the plant the damage starts. Learning to read these signs, then confirming with a soil or leaf test, lets you choose the right compost, mineral or microbe instead of guessing.

children.topic: How to read a sick plant
children.note: A simple field routine: look at where symptoms start, what pattern they form, and how they are spread across the field before deciding it is a nutrient problem.
First note whether the lower, older leaves or the young top leaves and growing tips are affected. This single clue splits nutrients into two groups.

manas.q: What is the first question to ask when diagnosing a deficiency?

children.note: Is the whole leaf pale, is yellowing only between the veins, are the margins burnt, or are there spots? Each pattern points to different nutrients.
A nutrient problem is usually gradual and follows soil type or management. Sharp patches, rows or a single spray swath suggest disease, pests, drainage or chemical injury.
Note pH, drainage, organic matter and recent weather. Many 'deficiencies' are really lock-outs caused by pH, waterlogging or cold soil.
A soil test and, where available, a leaf (tissue) test confirm what the eye suspects. Treat visual diagnosis as a hypothesis, not a verdict.

manas.q: Why should visual diagnosis be confirmed with a soil or leaf test?

children.note: After correcting, new growth should look normal within some weeks. Old damaged leaves rarely recover, so judge by new leaves.

A nutrient that can move inside the plant is shifted from old leaves to new growth when in short supply, so old leaves show signs first. An immobile nutrient stays put, so new leaves and tips suffer first.
These move readily in the phloem. When short, the plant robs older leaves to feed new growth, so lower leaves yellow, purple or scorch first.

manas.q: Which major nutrients are mobile, so their deficiency shows first on older leaves?

children.note: Molybdenum is moderately mobile and its shortage often looks like nitrogen deficiency on older and middle leaves, because Mo is needed to use nitrogen.
Calcium and boron barely move once placed in a leaf. Shortage shows at growing tips, young leaves, roots and fruit (e.g. blossom-end rot).

manas.q: Why does calcium deficiency show at growing tips and fruit rather than old leaves?

children.topic: Low mobility: Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu
children.note: These micronutrients move poorly, so symptoms such as yellowing between veins or small leaves appear on the youngest leaves.
Sulfur moves only partly, so S shortage usually shows as pale young leaves. This helps separate it from N shortage, which yellows old leaves first.

manas.q: How can you tell sulfur from nitrogen deficiency by leaf position?

children.note: Old leaves: N, P, K, Mg (and Mo). New leaves: Ca, S, Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B. Learn this split before learning individual symptoms.
The three nutrients crops take up in the largest amounts and the most common shortages in tropical soils.
How Nitrogen shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Whole plant pale green; older leaves turn yellow from the tip, then brown and die. Growth is slow and plants may mature early.

manas.q: What does nitrogen deficiency look like?

children.note: Common on low-organic-matter soils, after heavy rain that leaches nitrate, and where residues are burnt. Waterlogging and cold soils can mimic it.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Add well-made compost or FYM, grow legumes or green manure, and use N-fixers: Rhizobium for legumes, Azotobacter or Azospirillum for cereals and vegetables. Biofertilizers supply part of the need, not all of it.
How Phosphorus shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Plants are stunted and dark, with older leaves taking a purple or reddish tint, often on the underside. Roots and early growth are weak; flowering and maturity are delayed.

manas.q: Which microbes help correct phosphorus shortage?

children.note: P is locked up in both acidic soils (by iron and aluminium) and calcareous soils (by calcium). Cold soil and some hybrids also show purple tints without true P shortage.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Rock phosphate mixed into compost, together with phosphate-solubilising bacteria (PSB) that release P using organic acids. Mycorrhizal (AM) fungi extend roots to reach more P.
How Potassium shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Edges of older leaves turn yellow then scorch brown, as if burnt. Stems are weak and lodge, and fruit and grain quality is poor.
Typical on sandy, leached or eroded soils and under intensive cropping with no K returned. Drought scorch and salt damage can look similar.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Return crop residues, apply wood ash (sparingly, it raises pH) and K-rich compost. Potassium-mobilising bacteria (KMB/KSB) help release K held in soil minerals.
Needed in moderate amounts. Calcium and magnesium shortages are tied to acidic or sodic soils; sulfur to low organic matter.
How Calcium shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Growing tips of roots and shoots brown and die, young leaves are ragged or hooked, and fruit develops blossom-end rot (tomato, pepper).

manas.q: Which disorder in tomato fruit is linked to calcium shortage?

children.note: Common on acidic soils, but often caused by uneven watering because Ca travels with water flow. High K or sodium can compete with it.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) on acid soils, gypsum where pH need not rise, and steady irrigation and mulch to keep water flow even.
How Magnesium shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, giving a striped or herringbone look; leaves may turn reddish later.

manas.q: What does dolomite supply besides raising pH?

children.note: Acid, leached soils and heavy potassium or ammonium use, which compete with Mg uptake. Can be confused with virus mosaic.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Dolomitic lime corrects both acidity and Mg on acid soils. Compost and well-rotted manure add some Mg; avoid excessive K.
How Sulfur shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves are uniformly pale green to yellow, plants are thin and spindly. Oilseeds and brassicas are especially sensitive.
Low-organic-matter soils, residue burning and long use of fertilisers without sulfur. Easily confused with N shortage, which hits old leaves first.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Gypsum, compost and FYM supply S. Sulfur-oxidising bacteria (e.g. Thiobacillus) turn elemental sulfur into a plant-available form.
Needed in tiny amounts but essential. Most show on young leaves and are strongly affected by soil pH.
How Iron shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves turn yellow between the veins with veins sharply green; in severe cases new growth bleaches almost white.

manas.q: Why is iron chlorosis usually a lock-out rather than a lack of iron in the soil?

children.note: Rarely a true shortage of iron in soil; usually lock-out on calcareous, high-pH or waterlogged soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Lower pH locally with compost and sulfur, improve drainage, and use organic matter. Siderophore-producing bacteria such as Pseudomonas help chelate iron.
How Zinc shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Upper leaves show interveinal yellowing turning whitish; leaves are small and bunched into a rosette. In rice it causes browning ('khaira').

manas.q: What is ZSB and which deficiency does it address?

children.note: Calcareous soils, high-P soils, eroded soils where topsoil is lost, and flooded rice soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Zinc-solubilising bacteria (ZSB) release zinc from native soil compounds. Compost and FYM help; certifier-approved zinc sulfate is used when the soil truly lacks Zn.
How Manganese shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves get yellowing between veins with a speckled or mottled look; grey speck in oats is a classic form.
High-pH and calcareous soils, and very high organic matter. On very acid soils Mn can instead be toxic.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Correct pH toward neutral, add compost, and avoid over-liming. Healthy root microbes and mycorrhiza support Mn uptake.
How Boron shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Growing points die, young leaves are thick and distorted, flowers and fruit drop, and stems or roots crack (hollow stem in cabbage, cracked fruit).

manas.q: Why must boron be applied with great care?

children.note: Sandy and leached soils, and alkaline soils with free lime. Drought makes it worse. The gap between deficient and toxic levels is narrow.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Compost and organic matter hold boron; only tiny, measured doses of approved borax should be added. Never guess boron rates.
How Copper shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves are pale, twisted or dieback at the tips; cereals may have white, twisted leaf tips and empty ears.
Peat and very high organic matter soils bind copper; also sandy leached soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Usually corrected with small approved copper doses on proven-deficient soils. Compost from mixed sources supplies traces.
How Molybdenum shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Looks like nitrogen deficiency: older and middle leaves pale, margins may cup; 'whiptail' in cauliflower.

manas.q: Which micronutrient becomes more available when soil pH rises?

children.note: Strongly acidic soils lock Mo up; it is the one micronutrient that becomes more available as pH rises.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Liming acid soils often frees Mo. Legumes need Mo for Rhizobium to fix nitrogen, so poor nodulation can be a Mo signal.
Many problems mimic deficiencies. Rule these out before adding inputs.
Viral mosaics, wilts, root rots and leaf spots cause yellowing. Disease often shows lesions, spores, ooze, or a spreading patch rather than a symmetrical pattern.
Saturated soil starves roots of oxygen; plants yellow and wilt like N or Fe deficiency. Check drainage and smell for sour soil.
Dry soil stops nutrient flow to roots, causing leaf scorch like K shortage and calcium disorders in fruit.
The nutrient is present but unavailable because soil is too acid or too alkaline. Adding more fertiliser does little; fixing pH does.

manas.q: What is pH lock-out?

children.note: Twisted, cupped or strapped leaves, bleached new growth, or damage following a spray line or drift direction point to herbicide, not nutrition.

manas.q: What field clues suggest herbicide injury instead of deficiency?

children.note: Sucking pests cause stippling and bronzing; nematodes damage roots so plants look nutrient-starved. Check undersides of leaves and roots.
Hardpans, cutworms or transplant shock limit roots, so the plant cannot take up nutrients that are in the soil.
Too much fertiliser or saline water burns leaf edges and tips, looking like K deficiency.
The main organic and biological inputs, matched to the nutrient they support. They work best together with organic matter.
The base for every remedy: supply many nutrients slowly, feed soil microbes, improve water holding and buffer pH swings.
Legumes with Rhizobium add N; green manure crops add organic matter; Azolla with its cyanobacterial partner adds N in rice fields.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria for non-legumes such as cereals, millets and vegetables. They also produce growth hormones.

manas.q: Which bacteria fix nitrogen for non-legume crops?

children.note: Phosphate-solubilising bacteria release acids that dissolve rock phosphate and soil P. Enriching compost with both is a common practice.
Potassium-mobilising bacteria release K from soil minerals. They help where soil K reserves exist but are slowly available.
Zinc-solubilising bacteria free zinc already present in the soil. They do not create zinc where the soil truly has none.
Root-partner fungi whose threads reach far beyond roots, improving uptake of P, Zn and water.

manas.q: How do mycorrhizal fungi improve phosphorus uptake?

children.note: Lime raises pH and adds Ca; dolomite adds Ca and Mg; gypsum adds Ca and S without raising pH.
A source of K and Ca that also raises pH. Use small amounts and avoid on alkaline soils.
Contain traces of nutrients and growth substances. They support plants under stress but do not correct a serious deficiency alone.
Common errors when farmers try to fix yellow plants.
Yellowing has many causes: S, Fe, Mg, waterlogging, disease. Adding N to a non-N problem wastes money and can worsen pests.
If pH or drainage is the cause, inputs keep failing. Fix the soil condition first.
Biofertilizers need organic matter, moisture and correct pH. They complement nutrition; they rarely replace it fully on poor soils.

manas.q: Can biofertilizers alone always fix a severe deficiency?

children.note: Applying bacteria with fungicides, copper sprays or concentrated fertilisers can kill them before they act.
Boron, copper and zinc become toxic at high rates. Test, then apply small measured doses.
Local context for using these signs and remedies.
Many Kenyan highland soils are acidic, so P lock-out and Ca/Mg shortages are common; liming with soil-test guidance is often the first step.
Zinc and sulfur shortages are widespread in Indian soils; Soil Health Card testing helps identify them.
In Kenya, KALRO and private labs test soils; in India, Soil Health Card labs and KVKs do. Base decisions on results.
Use registered biofertilizers and approved minerals; organic farms must check permitted inputs with their certifier or PGS group.
Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.

nodeData.note: Organic fertilisers are manures, cakes, meals, green manures and natural minerals that feed crops through soil life. This map covers each source, how to calculate rates, storage, safety and what organic standards allow.

children.note: Organic fertilisers are nutrient sources of plant, animal or natural mineral origin, used with little processing. They feed both the crop and the soil life that releases the nutrients.

Bulky manures (farmyard manure, compost, green manure) are low in nutrients and used by the tonne, mainly for organic matter. Concentrated manures (oil cakes, bone, blood, fish meal) are richer and used in smaller amounts.

manas.q: What is the difference between bulky and concentrated organic manures?

children.note: Most of the nitrogen is in organic form. Soil microbes must first turn it into ammonium and then nitrate before roots can take it up, so supply is slower but lasts longer.

manas.q: Why do concentrated organic manures act slowly?

children.topic: Feed the soil, not only the crop
children.note: Besides N, P and K they add carbon, micronutrients and food for soil organisms, improving structure and water holding over time.
Dung and urine of livestock, often mixed with bedding. Nutrient content depends on the animal, its feed, the bedding and how the manure was stored.
Well-decomposed farmyard manure is low in nutrients, about 0.5% N, 0.2% P2O5 and 0.5% K2O in TNAU's table, but adds a lot of organic matter.

manas.q: Roughly how much N does well-rotted FYM contain?

children.note: The richest common manure: about 3.0% N, 2.6% P2O5 and 1.4% K2O. It ferments fast and, left exposed, can lose about half its nitrogen within a month.

manas.q: Which common manure is richest in N and P?

children.note: Pellets are fairly rich, about 3% N, 1% P2O5 and 2% K2O. Penning the flock on the field keeps the urine nutrients that pit storage loses.
Usually handled as slurry and quick to release nitrogen. Feed additives can leave copper and zinc in it, and it needs proper treatment because it carries pathogens and parasites.
Much of the potassium and quick nitrogen is in the urine. Bedding such as straw soaks it up; letting urine drain away wastes nutrients.
Partly rotted manure should go on 3–4 weeks before sowing; well-rotted manure can go on just before sowing. Large doses should be applied at least 15 days ahead to avoid nitrogen lock-up.

manas.q: When should partly rotted manure be applied before sowing?

children.note: Manure can carry E. coli O157, Salmonella, Listeria and Campylobacter. Several outbreaks linked to leafy greens have been traced to manure contamination.

manas.q: Name three disease bacteria that manure can carry.

children.note: Composting at thermophilic temperatures sharply reduces pathogen bacteria; a study on dairy manure found that keeping the heap hot for longer gave the largest reductions.

links.label: 📄 Thermophilic composting of dairy manure, Bioresource Technology 2016

children.note: Liquid manure, and the slurry left after biogas digestion, are quick-acting fertilisers that need careful handling to keep their nitrogen.
The material left after anaerobic digestion has turned part of the organic matter into biogas. Its make-up depends on what was fed into the digester.
Digestate is rich in nitrogen, much of it as ammonium. That makes it fast-acting but prone to ammonia loss if spread on the surface in sun and wind.

manas.q: Why should digestate be worked into soil quickly?

children.note: Apply close to the ground (band, trail hose, or by watering can at the base of plants) and cover or work it in soon. Avoid spraying it over leaves of food crops.
Separated digestate gives a liquid part used like a quick fertiliser and a fibrous solid part that can be composted or used as a soil conditioner.
Many East African dairy farms with zero-grazing units run small biogas digesters; the bioslurry is used on fodder, coffee, bananas and vegetables, often after drying or composting.
Digestion at normal (mesophilic) temperatures reduces but does not reliably remove pathogens, so treat digestate like manure near food crops.
Crops grown to be turned into the soil while green, mainly to add organic matter and, with legumes, nitrogen.
Sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea), dhaincha (Sesbania), cowpea, mucuna and lablab fix nitrogen with rhizobia and grow fast in warm climates.

manas.q: Name two legume green manure crops for warm climates.

children.note: Loppings from shrubs and trees grown elsewhere, such as Gliricidia, pongamia or Tithonia (common in Kenya), are cut and dug into the field.
Incorporate when the crop starts to flower, before stems turn woody, and wait a week or two for it to break down before sowing the next crop.

manas.q: At what stage should a green manure be turned in?

children.note: They add N and organic matter and smother weeds, but use a season, land and water. They work best fitted into a rotation or a short gap between crops.
The solid left after pressing oil from seeds. Non-edible cakes are mostly used as manure; edible cakes mostly go to cattle feed.
From neem seed kernels and covered by an Indian standard (IS 8558). Valued as manure and because it slows the conversion of ammonium to nitrate.

manas.q: Besides supplying N, what does neem cake do to soil nitrogen?

children.note: About 4.3% N, 1.8% P2O5 and 1.3% K2O. It contains ricin and is poisonous to animals, so store it away from livestock and dogs.

manas.q: Why must castor cake be kept away from livestock?

children.note: One of the richest cakes at about 7.3% N, 1.5% P2O5 and 1.3% K2O, but usually too valuable as feed to use as manure.
A non-edible cake with about 3.9% N, 0.9% P2O5 and 1.2% K2O, widely used in Indian horticulture.
Grind cakes finely for even spreading. Their nutrients become available roughly 7–10 days after application.

manas.q: How soon do nutrients from oil cakes become available?

children.note: Slaughterhouse and fish by-products: concentrated, slow to moderate release, and subject to animal by-product rules.
A phosphorus and calcium source: raw bone meal about 3–4% N and 20–25% P2O5, steamed about 1–2% N and 25–30% P2O5. It releases P best in acid soils.

manas.q: Which nutrient is bone meal mainly used for?

children.note: Dried blood with about 10–12% N and little P or K, one of the most concentrated organic nitrogen sources.

manas.q: About how much N does blood meal contain?

children.note: Fish meal holds about 4–10% N and 3–9% P2O5. Fish waste can also be composted or fermented into liquid fertiliser.
About 13% N, released slowly as microbes break down the keratin.
Feathers are mostly keratin protein and very high in N, but release it slowly unless they have been hydrolysed (steam-processed).
Use products processed under animal by-product rules, wear a dust mask, and keep bags closed: these meals attract dogs and rodents.
Natural rock powders, ash and marine materials that organic standards allow, each with limits.
Ground phosphate rock; ore grade varies from about 4% to 20% P2O5, and marketed rock is upgraded to 28% or more. It dissolves slowly and works best in acid soils.

manas.q: In which soils does rock phosphate work best?

children.note: Mostly calcium compounds plus potassium, so it acts as a liming material. Use only ash from untreated wood, in small doses, and avoid it on alkaline soils.

manas.q: Why should wood ash not be used on alkaline soils?

children.note: Accumulated droppings of seabirds or bats, high in N, P and K. Careless mining has destroyed seabird and cave habitats, so check the source.
Dried, ground seaweed supplies potassium, trace elements and soil-conditioning substances. Fresh seaweed should be rinsed or composted to reduce salt.
Worm-processed compost: a fine, stable manure. See the compost map for how to make it.
Urban organic wastes recycle nutrients but bring risks of heavy metals, plastics, drug residues and pathogens.
Sewage sludge is prohibited in certified organic production under the USDA rules and is not on the EU organic input list; India's NPOP likewise excludes it.

manas.q: Is sewage sludge allowed on certified organic farms?

children.note: The EU organic rules allow composted or fermented household waste only if it was separated at source and stays under strict heavy-metal limits.

links.label: 📄 Source: EU organic rules, Reg. 2021/1165 Annex II

children.note: EU organic rules exclude manure from factory farming. Certifiers may ask where bought-in manure comes from.

links.label: 📄 Source: EU organic rules, Reg. 2021/1165 Annex II

children.note: Urine is a clean, quick source of N and K used by some farmers after storage. Many organic standards do not allow human excreta, so check before using it on certified land.
Ask the certifier or national input list before buying any city compost or by-product, and keep the receipts and labels for inspection.
Work out what the crop needs, what the soil already supplies, and how much of the material's nutrients will become available this season.
Start from the crop's nutrient need and subtract what the soil test and the previous crop or green manure will supply.
Tables give typical values only; actual content varies with feed, bedding and storage. Have your own material analysed when you can.
Not all nutrients are released in the first season. For FYM, roughly 30% of N, 60–70% of P and 70% of K become available to the first crop.

manas.q: What share of FYM nitrogen is available to the first crop?

children.note: At 0.5% N, a tonne of FYM holds 5 kg N, of which about 1.5 kg is available in year one. Supplying 60 kg available N would need about 40 t/ha, which is why FYM is combined with richer sources.
At 7.3% N, one tonne of groundnut cake holds 73 kg N; 500 kg holds about 36 kg N. Split it between basal and top dressing.
Labels give phosphate as P2O5 and potash as K2O. Multiply P2O5 by 0.44 to get elemental P, and K2O by 0.83 to get K.

manas.q: How do you convert P2O5 to elemental P?

children.note: Manure rates set to meet nitrogen often supply far more P than the crop needs; over years this builds up and can wash into water.
TNAU suggests 10–20 t/ha of FYM, and more than 20 t/ha for fodder grasses and vegetables.

manas.q: What is a typical FYM dose per hectare?

children.note: Good storage keeps nutrients in the manure and out of water and air.
Shade and cover manure heaps so rain does not wash out nutrients and sun does not drive off ammonia; poultry manure is especially quick to lose N.
Keep heaps and slurry stores on a firm base, away from wells, streams and slopes that drain to water, because manure pathogens and nutrients move with runoff.

links.label: 📄 Manure pathogens and water, Int J Hyg Environ Health 2020

children.note: Store cakes and meals in sealed bags off the floor. Damp material goes mouldy, heats and attracts pests.
Organic does not mean harmless: manures and meals carry pathogens, toxins and gases.
US organic rules require raw manure to be worked in at least 120 days before harvest when the edible part touches soil, and 90 days for other food crops.

manas.q: How long before harvest must raw manure be applied under US organic rules (crops touching soil)?

children.note: Compost made from manure counts as treated if it reaches 55–77 °C for 3 days in a vessel or static pile, or for 15 days with 5 turnings in a windrow.

manas.q: What temperature range must organic compost reach?

children.note: Stirring slurry pits can release hydrogen sulfide and other dangerous gases. Never enter a pit, ventilate well, and fence pits away from children and animals.
Wear gloves and boots, wash hands before eating, and use a dust mask when spreading dry meals or poultry litter.
Common errors that waste nutrients or cause harm.
Too much manure leaches nitrate and builds up phosphorus just like synthetic fertiliser. Match the dose to crop need.
Fresh manure can scorch young roots with ammonia, lock up nitrogen while it decomposes and bring in weed seeds.
Uncovered heaps lose much of their nitrogen to the air and rain, leaving a low-value material.

In India, the Fertiliser Control Order sets specifications for organic manures such as city compost and vermicompost. In Kenya, fertilisers and soil conditioners sold commercially must meet KEBS standards.
Short videos from extension services, farmer-training groups and teachers.
A lecture on oil cakes, bone, blood and fish meal, guano and sludge.
Scotland's Farm Advisory Service on working out what organic fertilisers supply.
Scotland's Farm Advisory Service, a short clip on setting rates.
Access Agriculture: how a zero-grazing dairy unit feeds a biogas digester and the slurry goes back to the farm.
Access Agriculture farmer-training video.

children.topic: ▶ How to choose and sow green manure
children.note: Royal Horticultural Society guide to green manure crops.
Authoritative pages behind this map.
Nutrient tables and use of bulky and concentrated manures.
US organic regulation, including manure and compost rules.
Annex II lists the fertilisers and soil conditioners allowed in EU organic farming.
Review of how manure-borne bacteria survive and reach food crops.

nodeData.note: Biostimulants are substances and microbes that help crops use nutrients, tolerate stress or improve quality, without being fertilisers or pesticides. This map covers the main types, how they work, the evidence, how to use them and which are allowed in organic farming.

children.note: A product that helps the plant use nutrients, cope with stress or improve quality, through effects other than the nutrients it contains. It is neither a fertiliser nor a pesticide.

Under EU Regulation 2019/1009 a plant biostimulant stimulates plant nutrition processes independently of its nutrient content, aiming to improve nutrient use efficiency, abiotic stress tolerance, quality traits, or availability of nutrients confined in soil.

manas.q: What four aims does the EU definition of a biostimulant list?

children.note: The regulation splits biostimulants into microbial (category 6A) and non-microbial (category 6B) plant biostimulants.

manas.q: What are the two EU biostimulant categories?

children.note: For a CE-marked microbial biostimulant, the EU currently accepts only Azotobacter, mycorrhizal fungi, Rhizobium and Azospirillum.

manas.q: Which microbes may be used in an EU CE-marked microbial biostimulant?

children.note: The EU rules for CE-marked fertilising products, including biostimulants, have applied since 16 July 2022; products can still be sold under national rules instead.

A widely used classification lists humic and fulvic substances, protein hydrolysates, seaweed and plant extracts, chitosan and other biopolymers, inorganic compounds like silicon, beneficial fungi and beneficial bacteria.

manas.q: Name the main groups of biostimulants.

children.note: Dark, stable organic compounds formed when plant and animal matter decays over long periods; the main part of soil humus.
Humic acid dissolves in alkaline water but not in strong acid; fulvic acid dissolves at any pH and is smaller. Humin is the insoluble remainder.

manas.q: How do humic and fulvic acids differ in solubility?

children.note: Commercial products are mostly extracted with alkali from leonardite, lignite or peat; compost and vermicompost extracts are other sources.
Their chemical groups trigger hormone-like signalling in roots, which encourages root growth and nutrient uptake; the effect depends strongly on source and structure.

links.label: 📄 Humic substances as growth promoters, Molecules 2021

children.note: Usually applied to soil or through drip with fertiliser; fulvic products are also sprayed on leaves because they are smaller and soluble.
A few kilos of humic product per hectare are tiny next to the tonnes of organic matter in soil; compost and residues still build soil carbon.
The largest biostimulant group: liquid or soluble extracts of brown, red or green seaweeds, used mainly to help crops through stress.
A brown seaweed (knotted wrack) of the cold North Atlantic and the raw material for many extracts worldwide.

manas.q: Which brown seaweed is the most common raw material for extracts?

children.note: Kelps such as Ecklonia and Laminaria are also used, and in India sap from the cultivated red seaweed Kappaphycus is made into liquid biostimulants.
Polysaccharides such as alginate, laminarin and fucoidan, betaines, polyphenols, minerals and traces of plant hormones; none of these alone explains the effect.
Extracts made by alkaline, acid, enzyme or cold-pressing methods differ in composition, so two 'seaweed' products can behave differently.
Better tolerance of drought, heat, cold and salinity, with some effects on rooting, fruit set and quality.
Mixtures of free amino acids and peptides made by breaking down plant or animal proteins.
Plant sources include legume seeds and crop by-products; animal sources include collagen, leather waste, fish and feathers.

links.label: 📄 Colla et al. 2017, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Enzyme hydrolysis is gentle and keeps amino acids intact; strong acid or alkali hydrolysis is cheaper but can damage some amino acids and is not accepted by some organic standards.
Studies report better germination, growth and yield in many crops and relief from salinity, drought and heavy-metal stress.

manas.q: What stresses can protein hydrolysates help plants tolerate?

links.label: 📄 Colla et al. 2017, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Some peptides act as signals in the plant, nitrogen uptake can improve, and root exudates and microbes in the root zone change.

links.label: 📄 Colla et al. 2017, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: A natural polymer made by removing acetyl groups from chitin, mostly from crab and shrimp shells.
Chitin occurs in crustacean shells, insects and fungal walls; commercial chitosan is mostly made from crustacean waste.

manas.q: What is chitosan made from?

children.note: It is reported to promote root growth, to have antifungal, antibacterial and antiviral activity, and to trigger the plant's own defence responses.
Chitosans are classed as high, medium or low molecular weight, and the size affects how they work, so specify the type when comparing trials.
Because of its disease effects, chitosan is also regulated as a plant-protection substance in some regions; selling it with disease claims needs pesticide approval.
The second most abundant element in the earth's crust; not classed as essential but often beneficial, especially under stress.
Plants cannot use the silica (SiO2) of sand; they absorb silicon dissolved as silicic acid.

manas.q: In what form do plants take up silicon?

children.note: Grasses such as rice, sugarcane and wheat build up a lot of silicon; many dicots take up much less and respond less.
Reviews report that silicon can reduce damage from drought and salinity in many crops, but it is no cure-all.

links.label: 📄 Silicon for drought and salt stress, Frontiers in Plant Science 2020

children.note: Silica deposited in leaves and stems makes tissue harder to chew and pierce and can slow some fungal infections.
Calcium silicate slags, potassium silicate, rice husk ash and diatomaceous earth; returning rice straw also recycles silicon.
Living bacteria and fungi that improve nutrition or stress tolerance; many are also sold as biofertilisers.

links.label: 📄 Microbial inoculants as biostimulants: risk review, Life 2022

children.note: Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria such as Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Bacillus and Pseudomonas.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi extend the root system for P and water; Trichoderma also boosts root growth and defence.
Across 171 studies, biofertilisers raised yields most in dry climates (about 20%) and less in tropical (about 15%), oceanic and continental climates.

manas.q: In which climate did biofertilisers give the biggest yield gains?

links.label: 📄 Schütz et al. 2018, Frontiers in Plant Science (meta-analysis)

children.note: Check the count of live cells, expiry date and storage, and keep them away from chemical fungicides and bactericides.
Introducing large numbers of microbes needs strain identification and risk checks; reputable products name the strain.

links.label: 📄 Microbial inoculants as biostimulants: risk review, Life 2022

children.note: Extracts of land plants and fermented on-farm preparations with biostimulant-like effects.
Extracts of plants such as moringa leaves, licorice or garlic are studied for growth and stress effects; evidence is mostly small trials.
Jeevamrut, fermented plant juices and compost teas work partly as microbial and nutrient boosters; quality varies batch to batch.
Biostimulants act on the plant's own processes, and the effect is clearest when the crop is under stress.
They can raise antioxidants and protective compounds such as proline and betaines, helping cells survive drought, heat, cold and salt.

manas.q: Under what conditions do biostimulants show their clearest effect?

children.note: Many products increase root length and fine roots, so plants explore more soil for water and nutrients.

links.label: 📄 Humic substances as growth promoters, Molecules 2021

children.note: More roots, better uptake and more active root-zone microbes mean more of the applied nutrients end up in the crop.
Some products improve fruit set, sugar content, colour or shelf life; these claims need crop-specific evidence.
What independent analyses of many trials show, and their limits.
A meta-analysis of 180 open-field studies on non-microbial biostimulants found an average yield gain of 17.9%, largest when applied to soil.

manas.q: What average yield gain did the 2022 field meta-analysis find?

links.label: 📄 Li et al. 2022, Frontiers in Plant Science (meta-analysis)

children.note: Gains were biggest in arid climates and vegetables, and in soils low in organic matter, saline, sandy, nutrient-poor or not neutral in pH.

manas.q: In which soils were biostimulants most effective?

links.label: 📄 Li et al. 2022, Frontiers in Plant Science (meta-analysis)

children.note: Published trials tend to report successes, many are short or in pots, and many are funded by makers; a single farm may see no gain.
Use biostimulants as an extra on top of good basic management, not instead of it.
Fix nutrition, water, soil structure and pest control first; a biostimulant cannot make up for a missing nutrient.
Apply before or during predictable stress such as transplanting, flowering, heat or a dry spell, as the label directs.
Seed treatment, soil drench or drip, and foliar sprays in the cool morning or evening; follow the label rate.
Do a jar test before tank-mixing, and keep living microbial products away from copper, chemical fungicides and strong acids or alkalis.
Leave untreated strips beside treated ones, repeat in several places, and weigh the yield before deciding to buy again.

manas.q: How can a farmer test whether a biostimulant pays?

children.note: The market has many good products and many exaggerated ones.
Be wary of products that promise to replace fertiliser, cure diseases or double yields.
Ask for the raw material, extraction method, active content, batch analysis including heavy metals, and independent field trials in your crop.
A product that claims to control pests or diseases is a pesticide in law, needing registration by PCPB in Kenya or CIB&RC in India.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body registers products with pest or disease claims?

children.note: Since 2021 India's Fertiliser Control Order has a separate schedule for biostimulants, requiring data on efficacy and safety.

manas.q: Under which Indian law are biostimulants regulated?
